title: Where your money goes: value chains, channels and real costs
course_title: Agribusiness and Market Access: Grade, Store and Sell Your Produce for a Better Price

say: Where your money goes: value chains, market channels and your real costs.
This is the video for module one of Agribusiness and Market Access.
Every crop you sell travels a road before someone eats it. This road, with all its people, is called the value chain. It starts with you, the farmer.

say: Is the middleman simply stealing the difference? Let us look. These are illustrative numbers to show the method, not today's prices.

card.title: Where the money goes on 40 baskets

say: Hauwa receives 12,000 naira a basket, 480,000 naira in total.

card.title: Where the money goes on 40 baskets

say: The aggregator pays about 120,000 naira more for transport, loading and levies.

card.title: Where the money goes on 40 baskets

say: On the way, 6 baskets are crushed or spoil in the heat. He sells only 34, at 22,000 naira each, for 748,000 naira.

card.title: Where the money goes on 40 baskets

say: His margin is 148,000 naira, before his time and his risk. So most of the gap is transport, levies and lost baskets. Hauwa's best levers are cutting losses, sorting better produce, and selling in bulk with others.

say: Never compare the offered price. Compare the net price, what you keep after transport, levies, loading and rejected produce.

card.title: Three offers for 20 bags of maize

say: The farm gate offer of 55,000 naira a bag has no costs. Blessing keeps 1,100,000 naira.

card.title: Three offers for 20 bags of maize

say: The weekly market pays 62,000, but selling costs 2,000 a bag. She keeps 1,200,000 naira, with same-day cash.

card.title: Three offers for 20 bags of maize

say: The feed mill pays 66,000, minus 3,000 transport. It rejects 2 wet bags, which she sells later for less. She still keeps the most, 1,234,000 naira. But payment comes 14 days later.
If school fees are due tomorrow, the weekly market may suit her better.

card.title: Three offers for 20 bags of maize

say: When you sell to a new buyer, agree how and when you will be paid before anything is loaded. Watch the weighing, and ask what happens to produce they reject.
Do not release produce because of an SMS credit alert or a screenshot. Fake alerts are a common trick. Open your own bank or mobile money app and confirm the money has arrived.

say: You cannot tell whether a price is good if you do not know what the crop cost you. Count everything: land, ploughing, seed, fertiliser, hired labour, your own family's days, shelling, bags and transport.

card.title: Amina's cost per bag of maize
card.note: Illustrative figures. Use your own records.

say: Amina's season costs 850,000 naira.

card.title: Amina's cost per bag of maize
card.note: Illustrative figures. Use your own records.

say: She divides by her 25 bags. Her cost is 34,000 naira a bag.

card.title: Amina's cost per bag of maize
card.note: Illustrative figures. Use your own records.

say: For a 20% margin, she multiplies by 1.20. Her minimum is 40,800 naira a bag. Now, when a trader offers 38,000, she knows she covers costs but misses her target.

card.title: Amina's cost per bag of maize
card.note: Illustrative figures. Use your own records.

say: To remember. Much of the price gap is transport, levies and losses. Map your chain with dated prices. Compare the net price, never the offered price.
Confirm payment in your own app before loading. And know your cost per unit, because every decision depends on it.
The common mistake is forgetting family labour, land and bags.
